title: Booking Concert Tickets in Groups
description: Brute force to optimized: a segment tree over rows tracking both a minimum aggregate (for gather) and a sum aggregate (for scatter).

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Design a ticket booking system for a concert hall with n rows, each having m seats (numbered 0 to m-1). Support two operations: gather(k, maxRow) books k CONSECUTIVE seats in a single row, choosing the row with the smallest row number among rows 0 to maxRow that has enough free consecutive seats starting from the leftmost available position, and returns [row, firstSeat], or an empty array if impossible. scatter(k, maxRow) books exactly k seats (not necessarily consecutive or in the same row) somewhere among rows 0 to maxRow, filling seats row by row from left to right starting at the earliest available seat, returning true if successful (and performing the booking), or false (and changing nothing) if there is not enough total space.

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Find the leftmost row with enough free space\" repeatedly, over a prefix of rows","A segment tree over rows tracking the minimum occupied-seat-count, supporting a leftmost-match walk"],["\"Total free seats in a prefix of rows\"","A segment tree (or Fenwick tree) tracking the sum of occupied seats, supporting fast range-sum queries"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Each row starts empty (0 seats occupied). gather needs one row (among the allowed prefix) with enough trailing free space to hold k consecutive seats, picking the smallest such row number. scatter is more flexible: it can spread k seats across many rows in the allowed prefix, always filling the earliest available seats first, succeeding only if the total free space across those rows is at least k.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Theater Usher Filling Rows
blocks.text: Picture a movie theater where a group MUST sit together in one row (gather), versus a scattered set of solo moviegoers who will each take any open seat, filled row by row from the front (scatter). The usher needs to quickly answer "which row can fit this group" or "is there enough space total," without walking every row each time.

blocks.caption: gather picks the leftmost row (within the allowed prefix) with enough consecutive free seats

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: n=2 rows, m=5 seats each

blocks.content: {"headers":["Call","Result","Explanation"],"rows":[["gather(4, 0)","\"[0,0]\"","Row 0 has 5 free seats, books the first 4: seats 0-3."],["gather(2, 0)","\"[]\"","Row 0 now has only 1 free seat, not enough for 2 consecutive, and maxRow=0 forbids other rows."],["scatter(5, 1)","true","Row 0 has 1 free seat, row 1 has 5 free; fills row 0's last seat, then 4 seats of row 1, total 5."],["gather(2, 0)","\"[]\"","Row 0 is now completely full, so gather within maxRow=0 fails."]]}

blocks.text: 5. How Should We Think?

Before scanning rows one by one for every call, notice both operations reduce to range queries over a "seats occupied per row" array: gather needs "leftmost row in a prefix with occupied count <= m-k" (a minimum query plus a walk), and scatter needs "total occupied count in a prefix" (a sum query), both of which a segment tree answers in O(log n).

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: gather always books from the FRONT of a row (since it always starts from the leftmost free seat), so knowing only the current occupied-count per row is enough to know where a new consecutive booking would start and whether it fits.

Observation 2: For gather, finding "the first row (in a prefix) with occupied-count <= m-k" is exactly a segment-tree walk guided by the minimum occupied-count in each half, descending into the left child first whenever its minimum already satisfies the requirement.

Observation 3: For scatter, the total free space across a prefix of rows is (number of rows times m) minus (sum of occupied counts in that prefix), which a segment tree computes as a standard range-sum query.

Observation 4: Both operations then perform a point update (increasing one row's occupied count for gather, or several rows' counts for scatter) which the same segment tree supports in O(log n) per updated row.
This leads to a segment tree over the n rows, each leaf storing that row's occupied-seat count, supporting a leftmost-match walk (for gather) and range-sum queries plus updates (for scatter).
6. Brute Force Solution

Track each row's occupied-seat count directly in an array. For gather, scan rows 0 to maxRow linearly for enough space. For scatter, sum free seats across rows 0 to maxRow linearly, then fill row by row if enough space exists.
Step by step algorithm

items: Maintain seats[r] = number of occupied seats in row r (booking always fills from the left).
gather(k, maxRow): scan r from 0 to maxRow, return the first row with m - seats[r] >= k, booking [r, seats[r]] and incrementing seats[r] by k.
scatter(k, maxRow): sum (m - seats[r]) for r in 0..maxRow; if less than k, return false. Otherwise, fill rows in order, taking min(available, remaining) from each, until k seats are placed.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Both operations directly scan rows 0..maxRow, which is simple and correct but does not scale when n and the number of calls are both large.
The occupied-count-per-row representation is already correct for the final segment-tree version; only the scanning strategy needs to change.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n) per gather or scatter call in the worst case.
Space: O(n) for the seats array.

Limitation: with up to 5*10^4 rows and 5*10^4 calls, repeated O(n) scans can total O(n squared), which is too slow; a segment tree over rows answers both the "leftmost fitting row" and "total free space" queries in O(log n) per call.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
For gather: build a segment tree where each leaf stores a row's occupied-seat count, and each internal node stores the MINIMUM occupied count in its range. To find the leftmost row (within 0..maxRow) with occupied count <= m-k, walk the tree: at each node, check whether the left child's minimum already satisfies m-k; if so, recurse left (since we want the leftmost); otherwise recurse right.

For scatter: the same segment tree (or a second one) can answer range-SUM queries of occupied counts over 0..maxRow; subtracting from (maxRow+1)*m gives total free space, answering the feasibility check in O(log n) instead of a linear scan.

Updating: after a booking, a single point update (increase one row's occupied count, or several rows' counts one at a time) keeps both the minimum and sum aggregates correct in O(log n) per updated row.

The core idea: track the same per-row occupied counts as the brute force, but maintain them in a segment tree supporting O(log n) minimum-queries (with a leftmost-match walk) and sum-queries instead of linear scans.

Maintain a segment tree over the n rows where each node stores both the minimum and the sum of occupied counts in its range. gather uses a leftmost-match walk guided by the minimum; scatter uses a range-sum query for feasibility, then fills rows one at a time (bounded by how many distinct rows scatter can touch across all calls, which is capped by n overall).
9. Optimized Solution

blocks.caption: A segment tree over rows tracks min-occupied (for gather) and sum-occupied (for scatter)

blocks.text: Why This Works

The min-aggregate segment tree lets gather find the leftmost row satisfying "occupied <= m-k" without scanning every row: the walk always tries the left half first, only descending right if the left half's minimum proves no row there can fit. The sum-aggregate segment tree lets scatter answer "total free space in a prefix" in O(log n) rather than summing row by row, and the fill-row-by-row loop for the actual booking only ever touches rows that scatter fills to completion (each row can only be "completed" once across all scatter calls, bounding total work).

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(log n) per gather call; O(log n + rows touched) per scatter call, with total rows touched across all scatter calls bounded by O(n) overall.
Space: O(n) for the segment tree arrays.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Booking Concert Tickets in Groups shows how a single underlying array (occupied-count per row) can be wrapped in a segment tree tracking TWO different aggregates (minimum and sum) simultaneously, each serving a different query need.
Common Mistakes

items: Implementing gather to find ANY fitting row instead of the leftmost one, violating the required tie-breaking rule.
Forgetting that scatter must change nothing at all if the total free space is insufficient (a full rollback, not partial booking).

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["gather requesting exactly the number of free seats left in a row","Should succeed, since the requirement is at least k, not strictly more."],["scatter requesting exactly the total remaining free seats across the prefix","Should succeed, filling every remaining seat."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips

Explicitly separating the two aggregates the segment tree must maintain (minimum for gather's leftmost-match walk, sum for scatter's feasibility check) shows a clear understanding of why a plain single-purpose segment tree is not enough here.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "find the leftmost position satisfying a threshold", think: a segment tree tracking the minimum, walked left-first, descending right only when the left half cannot satisfy it.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you support cancelling a booking (freeing seats back up)?
How would you adapt this if rows had different capacities instead of a uniform m?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Any "find the leftmost/rightmost index in a range satisfying a threshold" problem, solved via a segment-tree walk guided by a min or max aggregate.
Range Sum Query - Mutable, using the same sum-aggregate segment tree technique as scatter's feasibility check.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The linear scan approach costs O(n) per call; the segment-tree approach costs O(log n) per gather call and O(log n) amortized per scatter call, using O(n) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: a segment tree over rows, maintaining both a minimum aggregate (for leftmost-match queries) and a sum aggregate (for range-total queries) simultaneously.
Core Idea: gather walks the min-tree leftmost-first; scatter checks total free space via the sum-tree, then fills rows directly.
Time: O(n) per call for the linear scan, O(log n) per gather and amortized O(log n) per scatter for the segment-tree approach.
Space: O(n) for the segment tree arrays.
Most Important Observation: the same per-row occupied-count array can support two different fast aggregate queries (min and sum) when wrapped in a segment tree.
Interview Difficulty: a genuinely hard design problem, combining two segment-tree query types under one data model.
One line memory trick: min-tree for "find the leftmost fitting row," sum-tree for "is there enough space total."
